$comment: Desk briefings: what to know before each activity. ideas/formula/concepts are for Advanced (concept ids come from the lesson terms in src/data/learn/units). entry is a simpler version for Entry players, given for every activity that has an Entry mode. Checked by tests/learn.test.ts.

ideas: Profit = revenue − costs. Every dumpling you make but don't sell is a cost with no revenue.
Weather and competitors move demand: make fewer on rainy nights, more when the street is busy.
A lower price sells more, but each sale earns less. Watch the profit, not the number sold.
An upgrade is worth buying if the extra profit over the remaining nights beats its price.
night-market.formula: profit = price × units sold − cost per unit × units made − stall costs
entry: Profit is the money you make minus the money you spend.
Make enough snacks to sell, but not so many that you waste them.
If nobody is buying, try a lower price.

ideas: Buy where a good is cheap and sell where demand is high: that's arbitrage.
Selling lots in one port pushes the price down, so spread your sales.
Count shipping costs: the gap between the two prices must be bigger than the cost of moving the goods.
harbor-trading.formula: profit per crate = sell price − buy price − shipping cost
entry: Buy things where they are cheap and sell them where they cost more.
If you sell too many in one place, the price drops.

ideas: Fixed costs stay the same however much you sell: rent, salaries, insurance.
Variable costs rise with every unit: ingredients, packaging, shipping per order.
Ask: if we sold twice as much next month, would this cost double?
entry: Some costs stay the same every month, like rent.
Some costs grow when you sell more, like ingredients.

ideas: Income statement: revenue − cost of goods sold = gross profit; minus operating expenses = operating profit; minus taxes = net income.
The balance sheet must balance: assets = liabilities + equity.
Ledger errors are often a swapped digit, a missing entry or an entry on the wrong side.
accounting.formula: assets = liabilities + equity; net income = revenue − all costs
entry: Add up every receipt carefully, one at a time.
If the total looks wrong, check each number again to find the mistake.

ideas: Each sale first covers its own variable cost; the rest is the contribution margin.
Break-even is the number of sales where contribution margin covers all fixed costs.
Higher prices or lower variable costs cut the break-even point; higher fixed costs raise it.
break-even.formula: break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost)
entry: To break even, the money you earn must equal the money you spend.
Each sale helps pay for things like rent.

ideas: Faster deliveries earn bigger tips, but every metre costs fuel: a variable cost per trip.
Plan the shortest route that hits every order before it goes cold.
Your real earnings are tips minus fuel.
entry: Deliver the food fast to get bigger tips.
Driving uses fuel, so pick short routes.

ideas: A stand has fixed costs (the stand, a permit) and variable costs (lemons, cups).
Price for profit, not just for sales.
Save some profit to grow, instead of spending it all.
entry: Running a stand costs money for lemons and cups.
Save some of what you earn to make your stand better.

ideas: Profit = revenue − costs. Margin = profit ÷ revenue.
Gross margin uses only the direct cost of what was sold; profit margin uses every cost.
Read each question for which costs it counts.
entry: Profit is money earned minus money spent.
Count every cost before working out the profit.

ideas: Questions cover running a business, trade and how prices are set.
Profit = revenue − costs; prices rise when demand beats supply.
Read each question twice, then eliminate the clearly wrong answers.
entry: These questions are about businesses and buying and selling.
Take your time and read each answer.

ideas: First find the exposure: will this business buy the commodity later (hurt if prices rise) or sell it (hurt if prices fall)?
Hedge in the opposite direction: buyers buy futures, sellers sell futures, a stock portfolio sells index futures.
Size the hedge: exposure ÷ contract size, or beta × portfolio value ÷ (index level × multiplier) for a fund.
Gains and losses settle daily, so keep enough cash to meet margin calls.
Franchise profit = sales − costs − royalty; payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly cash profit.
Value the rival as a whole business: EBITDA × the multiple similar chains sold for.
Bridge to what the shares are worth: subtract net debt (debt − cash).
Set your top bid before bidding and stick to it.
Air is fast and dear, ocean slow and cheap, rail in between.
Slow shipping ties up the goods' value: carrying cost = value × yearly rate × days ÷ 365.
Arriving late can lose sales, so add the expected cost of lateness.
Pick the mode with the lowest landed cost, not the lowest freight.
supply-chain.formula: landed cost = freight + value × rate × days ÷ 365 + chance late × cost of lateness
entry: Planes are fast but cost more. Ships are slow but cheap.
Pick the way that gets things there in time for the lowest cost.

ideas: Sole proprietors and general partners are personally liable for the business's debts.
LLCs protect owners and pass profit through to their personal returns, taxed once.
Corporations pay corporate tax, then dividends are taxed again, but they can sell shares to investors.
Self-employed owners pay both halves of FICA: about 15.3%.
biz-structure.formula: owner keeps = profit × (1 − corporate rate) × (1 − dividend rate)

ideas: Compare unit prices, not shelf prices: price ÷ size.
Coupons and multi-buy deals only help if you need the item and quantity.
Stay under budget first, then pick the best value.
entry: Buy everything on your list without going over your money.
If two items are the same, pick the cheaper one.

ideas: Stacked discounts multiply: 20% then 10% off is 28% off, not 30%.
BOGO is 50% off each only if you need two.
A big 'original price' is an anchor: judge the price you'd actually pay.
entry: Work out the price after the sale.
The lower final price is the better deal.

ideas: Change = amount paid − price.
Count up from the price to the amount paid, biggest notes and coins first.
Fewest pieces: always use the largest coin or note that still fits.
entry: Change is the money you give back.
Start with the biggest coins and bills you can.

ideas: Amount received = amount × rate − fees.
A 'no commission' booth can still hide its fee in a worse rate.
Compare what you actually receive from each booth.
entry: Each country has its own money.
Multiply your dollars by the rate to see how many pounds you get.

ideas: Renting: rent grows each year, but your down payment stays invested.
Buying: mortgage interest, property tax, insurance and upkeep, but the home may appreciate.
The down payment's lost investment return is a real cost: opportunity cost.
Short stays usually favour renting; long stays can favour buying.
entry: Renting means paying to live in someone else's home.
Buying means you own the home, but it costs a lot upfront.

ideas: Build the budget from take-home pay, not gross.
50/30/20: needs, wants, then saving and debt.
Surprises will come: an emergency fund and sinking funds keep them off a credit card.
budget-planner.formula: needs 50% · wants 30% · saving 20% of net pay
entry: A budget is a plan for your money.
Pay for needs first, then save some, then have fun with the rest.

ideas: Split money the moment you earn it: pay yourself first.
Saving is for future goals, spending for now, sharing for others.
Even small regular amounts add up.
entry: Put some money in each jar: save, spend and share.
Saving a little every time helps a lot later.

ideas: Questions cover budgets, prices, deals and currencies.
Unit price = price ÷ quantity; stacked discounts multiply.
For currencies: amount × rate − fees.
entry: These questions are about budgets, prices and money from other countries.
Read each answer before you pick.

ideas: Bond prices move opposite to yields.
A coupon above market yields means a premium price; below means a discount.
Duration estimates the price move: −duration × change in yield.
Credit spread = corporate yield − government yield: the reward for default risk.
You quote a bid and an ask: a tight spread wins the client, a wide spread earns more.
Every deal leaves you holding currency risk: hedge it in the market or carry it.
Cross rates must agree: A/C = (A/B) × (B/C). If a loop of three trades ends with more money, that's triangular arbitrage.
Start from each client's goal and time horizon: short goals need safety, long ones can take risk.
Check the expected return meets the goal and the volatility fits how much loss they can bear.
A retiree living on a portfolio needs a sustainable withdrawal rate, around 4%.
Inflation from a basket = sum of (weight × price change).
Inelastic demand means a small supply shock causes a big price jump.
Futures above spot is contango; below is backwardation.
Real return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.
Gross margin shows pricing power: (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue.
Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ inventory; days of inventory = 365 ÷ turnover. Faster is usually healthier.
Same-store sales show whether existing shops are really growing.
Make the call on the whole picture, not one metric.
Each candle shows the open, high, low and close.
Price above a rising moving average suggests an uptrend; volume shows conviction.
Real markets are close to unpredictable, so bet small when unsure.
entry: The chart shows if the price went up or down.
Nobody can always guess right, so think it through.

ideas: Questions cover stocks, bonds, funds, risk and return.
Higher expected return comes with higher risk; diversification cuts single-company risk.
Bond prices fall when rates rise.
entry: These questions are about stocks and saving for the future.
Take your time with each one.

ideas: An asset is something you own that has value.
A liability is something you owe.
Net worth = assets − liabilities.
entry: Something you own is an asset.
Money you owe is a liability.

ideas: Cash is safe but loses to inflation; stocks swing but grow most over long periods.
An index fund spreads risk across many companies; hot stocks concentrate it.
Judge the result in real terms: did it beat inflation?
entry: Different baskets grow in different ways.
Mixing things together is safer than picking just one.

ideas: Dollar-cost averaging invests a fixed amount each month, so you buy more shares when prices are low.
Timing the market means guessing tops and bottoms, which almost nobody does reliably.
Average cost = total invested ÷ total shares.
dca-lab.formula: average cost = total invested ÷ shares bought
entry: Putting in the same amount every month is a calm way to invest.
When prices are low, your money buys more.

ideas: Questions get harder as you climb: interest, investing and the economy.
Know the rule of 72, compound interest and how inflation hits real returns.
Two out of three on each floor gets you up.
entry: Answer questions to climb the tower.
Get two out of three right to go up.

ideas: Ask which company the news actually touches: the one named, its suppliers, its rivals.
Prices react to surprises, not to news everyone expected.
Some headlines barely matter to the stock at all.
entry: Is this news good or bad for the company?
Good news often makes a company's price go up.

ideas: Most startups fail and a few pay off big, so judge each bet by its expected value.
Spread small amounts across several startups instead of betting everything on one.
Only invest money you can afford to lose.
entry: New businesses are exciting, but many don't work out.
Only use money you can afford to lose.

ideas: High returns with no risk are a red flag.
Pressure to act now, secret methods and guaranteed profits signal hype or fraud.
Reasonable claims talk about risk, time and diversification.
entry: If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
Real investing takes time and has ups and downs.

ideas: Discount each year's free cash flow at the WACC.
Add a terminal value for the years after: last cash flow × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g), discounted too.
Enterprise value − net debt = equity value; ÷ shares = fair value per share.
More than 15% upside is a Buy, more than 15% downside a Sell, otherwise Hold.
valuation-desk.formula: fair value per share = (EV − net debt) ÷ shares

ideas: Assets are owned, liabilities are owed, equity is what's left for the owners.
The sheet balances: assets = liabilities + equity.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (above 1.5 is comfortable).
Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ equity (higher is riskier).
Warning signs: profits that never turn into cash, receivables growing faster than sales, insiders selling.
Short profit = (sell price − buy-back price) × shares − borrow fee.
A short's loss is unlimited if the price keeps rising, and squeezes happen.
short-desk.formula: short profit = (sell − buy back) × shares − borrow fee

ideas: Five warm-up questions on money, needs and wants, saving and banks.
Narwhal explains every answer, so read the explanations.
entry: Five easy questions about money.
Narwhal will help with every answer.

ideas: Questions come from every topic: saving, banking, budgeting, earning and interest.
Answer quickly for a time bonus, but accuracy matters more.
entry: A game show with questions about money.
Answer quickly for bonus points.

ideas: Count each deposit carefully: notes first, then coins.
Every deposit adds to the account balance; keep the records straight.
entry: Count the money each customer brings.
Start with the bills, then the coins.

ideas: Pay on time every month: payment history is the biggest part of the score.
Keep credit utilization under 30%, ideally under 10%.
Avoid lots of new applications, and keep old accounts open.
Paying in full avoids interest without hurting your score.
entry: Borrowing is like making a promise to pay back.
Paying back on time shows people they can trust you.

ideas: Taxes pay for public goods that serve everyone: roads, schools, police, parks.
Families pay for their own private things: groceries, phones, holidays.
Some things are shared, like public transport fares plus tax support.
entry: Taxes pay for things everyone shares, like parks and schools.
Families pay for their own things, like toys and food.

ideas: Catch money, dodge the fees.
Fees are small but they add up, just like real ones.
entry: Catch the falling money!
Stay away from the red bills.

ideas: Match each money word to its meaning.
Remember where cards are to make fewer misses.
entry: Find the matching pairs.
Try to remember where each card is.

ideas: Pick the better deal in one second: compare unit prices, not just the sticker.
Watch for sizes: a bigger pack isn't always cheaper per unit.
entry: Tap the cheaper price as fast as you can.
Look carefully at both numbers.

ideas: Needs first: food, vet care and basic supplies.
Then fun extras with what's left.
Don't go over the budget.
entry: Pay for what your pet needs first, like food.
Then pick fun extras if there's money left.

ideas: Compare the total cost, not just the monthly payment.
Loans add interest; leases are cheap monthly but you own nothing at the end.
Cars lose value as they age, so resale value matters.
car-deal.formula: total cost = all payments + upfront costs − resale value
entry: Look at the price and how much you pay every month.
The lowest monthly payment isn't always the best deal.

ideas: Down payment = price × down payment %; the loan is the rest.
Monthly payment: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−N) with i = APR ÷ 12.
Total interest = payment × months − loan. A calculator is allowed.
entry: A home loan is paid back a little every month.
Paying more at the start means borrowing less.

ideas: Split the trip budget across travel, hotel, food and fun.
Book the big fixed costs first, then plan daily spending.
Leave a little for surprises.
entry: Plan how much to spend on travel, sleeping, food and fun.
Keep a little money for surprises.

ideas: Do the job well to get paid.
Earned money is gross pay; in Advanced, taxes come out first.
entry: Do a good job to earn money.
Doing it well gets you paid more.

ideas: Market orders fill now and pay the spread; limit orders wait in the queue at your price.
Watch the order book: heavy bids under the price and thin asks above often push it up.
Stay inside the position limit and finish flat, holding nothing at the end.
order-book.formula: spread = ask − bid; profit = (sell − buy) × shares

ideas: Percent move = (new − old) ÷ old.
1 basis point = 0.01%; 100 bp = 1%.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate. P/E = price ÷ EPS.
Cross rates: A/C = (A/B) × (B/C).
Match terms to definitions: P/E, Sharpe, beta, duration, EBITDA and more.
Read the Glossary first if any term is new.
Fewer misses and a faster time score more.
Set prices for profit: price × visits − cost per visit, not the most visits.
Hire a vet only if the extra profit beats their pay.
Billing insurers directly can bring more patients, but you wait to be paid: profit isn't cash.
Keep enough cash to cover wages while receivables come in.
vet-practice.formula: profit = (price − variable cost) × visits − fixed costs

ideas: An adaptive test across every topic: right answers move you up a level, wrong ones down.
Don't guess wildly: the result is used to suggest lessons.
Use the Glossary afterwards for any terms that came up.
Convert costs with the exchange rate, then add fees.
Compare cards by foreign transaction fees; always decline dynamic currency conversion.
Price travel insurance by expected value, but remember the big rare bills.
Debt-to-income = (existing payments + new loan payment) ÷ monthly income. Above about 36% is a warning.
Higher credit scores and collateral mean lower default risk and lower losses.
Approve at prime for strong borrowers, price for risk in the middle, decline the worst.
Your score is the expected profit of the whole loan book.
loan-officer.formula: expected profit ≈ (1 − PD) × interest margin − PD × loss given default

ideas: Property tax = assessed value × rate: the city's main income.
Services have diminishing returns: spread money where the next dollar does most.
Recessions cut revenue while needs rise; plan reserves.
Borrow with municipal bonds for long-lived projects, not running costs.
Do the skill game well to earn the shift's pay; good shifts lead to promotions.
Gross pay is before tax; net pay is what you keep.
In Advanced, FICA and income tax come out of each paycheck.
entry: Pick a job and try your best.
Doing well can get you a promotion.

ideas: Research the market rate, set your target and your walk-away point.
Counter with evidence: skills, results and market data.
Stay polite and remember benefits and bonuses are negotiable too.
entry: It's OK to ask for fair pay.
Be polite and explain why you're worth it.

ideas: An option lets you buy shares at the strike price; it's worth share price − strike if that's positive.
Options vest over time, often with a 1-year cliff.
If the company doesn't do well, options can be worth nothing while salary is certain.
stock-options.formula: option value = max(0, share price − strike) × vested options
entry: Some jobs give you a tiny piece of the company.
It's worth more if the company does well.

ideas: Plan the robot's path before you start.
Fewer commands means more freelance pay.
Freelance pay has no tax taken out, so set some aside.
entry: Give the robot directions to reach the coins.
Try to use as few steps as you can.

ideas: Needs keep you safe, healthy and able to work or study.
Wants are nice extras.
Some items depend on the situation: a phone may be a need for work.
entry: A need is something you must have, like food.
A want is something nice to have, like a new toy.

ideas: Your first paycheck is net pay: taxes have already come out.
Pay yourself first, then plan needs and wants.
Start an emergency fund before spending on extras.
entry: Plan what to do with your first pay.
Save some before you spend.

ideas: Check the sender's real address and the real link before clicking.
Urgency, threats and requests for codes or passwords are red flags.
Real companies never ask for your password or a code by message.
entry: Some messages try to trick you.
Never share passwords or codes.

ideas: Length beats complexity: a long passphrase is stronger than a short jumble.
Never reuse passwords across sites.
Turn on two-factor authentication for important accounts.
entry: Long passwords are stronger.
Use a different password for each account.

ideas: Taxable income = income − the larger of the standard or itemized deductions.
Apply the brackets slice by slice, then subtract credits.
Refund = tax withheld − tax owed (negative means you owe).
entry: Taxes help pay for things everyone uses.
Everyone who earns money pays a share.

ideas: Gross − FICA − income tax − deductions = net pay.
FICA is 7.65% of gross.
Effective tax rate = total tax ÷ gross. Check hours × rate to spot payroll mistakes.
paycheck-decoder.formula: net = gross − FICA − income tax − deductions
entry: Your pay before anything is taken out is called gross pay.
What you actually get to keep is called net pay.

ideas: Questions cover jobs, paychecks, taxes and staying safe online.
Net pay = gross − taxes − deductions.
Real companies never ask for passwords or codes.
entry: Questions about jobs, pay and staying safe online.
Read each answer carefully.

ideas: Post-money = pre-money + investment; the investor owns investment ÷ post-money.
Each round dilutes earlier owners: old % × (1 − new investor %).
At a sale, preferred investors take the larger of their money back or their share; common holders split the rest.
Each customer should be worth well over what they cost to win: LTV ÷ CAC of 3 or more.
LTV ≈ monthly margin ÷ monthly churn; CAC = marketing spend ÷ new customers.
A free trial lifts sign-ups but delays revenue; watch the conversion rate.
Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn: don't run out of cash.
fintech-lab.formula: LTV ≈ monthly margin ÷ churn; runway = cash ÷ burn

ideas: Trend-following works in trending markets; mean reversion in choppy ones.
Compare against buy-and-hold on Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown, not raw return.
Include trading costs, and trust only the out-of-sample test: over-tuned rules fail on new data.
Block when chance of fraud × amount is bigger than the cost of upsetting a good customer.
Missed fraud costs the full amount; false alarms cost customer friction.
Precision = fraud caught ÷ all blocks; recall = fraud caught ÷ all fraud.
fraud-ops.formula: block if P(fraud) × amount > P(genuine) × friction cost

ideas: Compound interest grows faster the longer it runs.
More frequent compounding and regular top-ups make the tree grow faster.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate.
entry: Money in savings grows a little every year.
The longer you wait, the more it grows.

ideas: Starting early beats saving more later, thanks to compounding.
Always get the full employer match: it's free money.
Roth if your tax rate is lower now, traditional if it's higher now.
entry: Saving early gives money more time to grow.
The friend who starts first ends up with more.

ideas: Premium is paid every month; the deductible is paid when you claim.
Lower premium usually means a higher deductible.
Insure disasters you couldn't afford; self-insure small losses.
entry: Insurance helps pay when something bad happens.
You pay a little every month to be protected.

ideas: Build 3 to 6 months of essential costs in cash.
Without a fund, surprises go on high-interest cards.
Top the fund back up after you use it.
emergency-fund.formula: months of cover = fund ÷ monthly essentials
entry: A rainy-day jar is money saved for surprises.
Fill it before you need it.

ideas: Monthly payment: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−N), i = APR ÷ 12.
Total cost = all payments + fees; compare that, not the monthly payment.
Extra payments go straight to principal and cut the interest.
entry: Some loans cost more in the end than others.
Add up everything you pay back to compare.

ideas: Legit charities are registered and say what they achieve.
Pressure to give now, cash-only requests and vague goals are red flags.
A low overhead isn't the same as high impact.
entry: Real charities tell you what they do with the money.
Be careful if someone rushes you to give.

ideas: Questions cover saving, compounding, retirement, insurance and giving.
Compound interest and starting early do the heavy lifting.
Insure disasters, self-insure small losses.
entry: Questions about saving, growing money and helping others.
Take your time.

ideas: Portfolio return is the weighted average of the assets' returns.
Portfolio risk depends on correlation: low correlation cuts risk the most.
The best Sharpe ratio gives the most return per unit of risk.
Keep the fund's real value: payout should be at or below the expected real return.
Judge the plan on bad scenarios, not just the average: early crashes hurt most.
Diversify across assets to protect the downside.
Never miss a payment: that's the first goal.
Cheapest order: cut wants, use emergency cash, then low-cost credit; high-interest debt and selling investments last.
Selling investments after a crash locks in the loss.
stress-test.formula: months of cover = savings ÷ monthly essentials

ideas: Compare charities by cost per outcome, not overhead.
A deductible gift really costs gift × (1 − marginal rate).
Giving appreciated shares also avoids capital gains tax; matching gifts double the impact.
A donor-advised fund takes the deduction now and grants later.
impact-desk.formula: real cost of a gift = gift × (1 − marginal rate)
